summary:
Grenada criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 431 of the Criminal Code, covering "unnatural crime," carries a maximum of ten years' imprisonment for male same-sex acts. Section 430 addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men, and a gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. Both provisions remain in force.

United States Department of State reporting for 2023 states that the criminalising laws are not enforced in practice, and records no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances in Grenada that year.

No legal gender recognition is available. A trans visitor's passport or other documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth or by another jurisdiction, with no domestic procedure to amend it.

Neither the 1973 Constitution, which contains no equality or privacy clause, nor any statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTIQ people in Grenada face discrimination in housing, education, employment and access to public services.

Fear of prosecution under the criminal provisions inhibits LGBTIQ people from reporting crimes to the police, which reduces the practical protection police provide.

Grenada does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or registered partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, stating that "the day is fast approaching" for repeal. No legislative repeal has followed.

GrenCHAP, a local civil-society organisation, has for more than fifteen years provided services to marginalised groups including LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, as documented in a joint stakeholder report by The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali and GrenCHAP submitted for the 2024 Universal Periodic Review.
tangentialFactors:
Grenada's legal framework is characteristic of a penal code retained from the colonial era, with the criminal provisions framed in terms of morality rather than age of consent or public order enforcement. The 2023 United States Department of State assessment that the laws are unenforced suggests the practical risk of prosecution is low, but the offences remain available for use.

The absence of any equality or privacy clause in the 1973 Constitution weakens the basis for constitutional challenge to the criminal provisions or to discrimination, since no explicit fundamental right is breached by them.

The May 2013 statement by the President of the Senate indicates that repeal has been raised at the level of the presiding officer of one chamber of Parliament, but this constitutes political signalling rather than legislative change.

Grenada participates in the United Nations Universal Periodic Review, and in October 2024 non-governmental stakeholders submitted a report documenting the country's LGBTIQ+ legal and social situation for that process, indicating an active, if small, domestic advocacy infrastructure.

Outright International's regional programme covering the Americas includes Grenada among the jurisdictions it monitors, placing the country within a Caribbean subregional group where decriminalisation litigation and reform have been contested in several neighbouring states, though specific outcomes elsewhere are not sourced here.
localsOnly:
Residents who have sex or intimacy that falls within Sections 430 or 431 remain technically exposed to prosecution, and the absence of legal gender recognition means Grenadian trans people live with the sex marker recorded on their birth documentation with no domestic route to change it.

Grenadian residents cannot enter a legally recognised same-sex partnership or marriage, and same-sex couples have no claim to the property, immigration, hospital-visitation or inheritance rights attached to opposite-sex marriage.

Workers, tenants, students and patients have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no constitutional equality or privacy clause to invoke.

GrenCHAP operates locally with more than fifteen years of service history, providing support to LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, and functions as a principal point of contact for community members needing assistance or referrals.

The social environment is reported as one in which LGBTIQ people face discrimination not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents, and in which the criminal code is a known deterrent to reporting victimisation to police.
outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty documented here applies to Section 431. The specific penalty range attached to Section 430, and to the gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision, is not sourced in the available inventory and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses how Grenada handles trans people in immigration screening, in detention, or in access to gender-affirming healthcare. Whether any such policy exists is unresolved rather than absent.

The claim that the criminalising laws are unenforced rests on a single reporting year (2023) from one government's human rights report. No prosecution or acquittal statistics covering other years are available here, and the durability of the non-enforcement pattern is unresolved.

The 2013 call by the President of the Senate for reconsideration of the ban is documented as a public statement; whether any bill, parliamentary motion or official review followed it is unresolved in this inventory.

No data is available on hate-motivated violence against trans people in Grenada, on police handling of complaints from LGBTIQ victims, or on whether GrenCHAP's services include trans-specific care beyond the categories listed in the stakeholder report.
